ev.q: This report describes a family of five whose BLLs above CDC’s BLRV were associated with use of surma.
child B’s BLL had declined from 18 to 14 μ g/dL, child C’s from 30 to 22 μ g/dL
In September 2012, routine testing detected a BLL of 15 μ g/dL in an asymptomatic child, aged 4 years (child A)
It had taken approximately 5 years for the BLLs of child B and child C to decline to levels <5 μ g/dL.

comparison.referent: CDC blood lead reference value (3.5 μg/dL)

ev.q: Blood lead levels of a mother and her four children with a history of surma use — New York City, 2012–2023*
Two years later, in 2018, BLLs in child B and child C continued to decline (4 μ g/dL and 6 μ g/dL, respectively).
Child B’s BLL at that time was 18 μ g/dL.
A surma sample was obtained, tested, and found to contain 390,000 ppm of lead.

public_health_question.v: What was the source and course of elevated blood lead levels in a New York City mother and her four children over 11 years?

ev.q: Over a period of 11 years, four other family members, including the child’s mother and three younger siblings, were also affected.

determinants_of_health.v: deeply ingrained cultural practices; blood lead testing mandates

ev.q: challenges of risk communication when deeply ingrained cultural practices, such as the use of surma, persist despite health warnings
effectiveness of blood lead surveillance depends on testing mandates, and might miss populations at risk of lead exposure

notes: Single-family case series; BLLs above the BLRV define cases (a classification cutpoint), so the comparison recorded is the series of BLLs over time, set side by side. No statistical methods.
